note: The ellipsis char … (U+2026) is a sentence terminator for capitalization.
Leading uppercase avoids first-letter-cap noise; isolates the space-collapse rule.
The (?!\d) lookahead protects number groups like 3,14 from getting a space.
Decimal 2.5 is shielded so its dot is not a sentence boundary.
A full URL survives post-process intact (no punctuation/cap mangling inside).
A trailing '.' is split off the URL so it still ends the sentence, URL stays intact.

mailto: has no // authority so the URL rule misses it; it must be shielded before the EMAIL pass so the whole href survives instead of a bare 'mailto:' getting a space injected after its colon (spintax-js#41).
The production bug: the email shield carved contact@example.com out of the href, leaving 'mailto:' whose colon then got a space, producing a malformed 'mailto: contact@…' link.
A trailing '.' is split off the mailto: URI (like URLs) so it still ends the sentence and caps the next word, address intact.
tel: URI shielded before the 'space after colon' rule can split 'tel:' from its number.
Domain is shielded; the '.' after it still ends the sentence and caps the next word.
Single-token abbreviation 'соц.' is whitelisted, so 'сети' is NOT falsely capitalized.
'Mr.' is whitelisted, so 'smith' is not treated as a new sentence.

Multi-dot abbreviation 'e.g.' (2+ dotted groups) is shielded by step 5a. Its \b is PHP's under /u — PCRE2_UCP, a letter of any script is a word character — so a Cyrillic 'т.д.' is shielded the same way (postprocess/ru-multidot-abbreviation). This note used to say the opposite, and every tree-walk engine mangled 'т.д.' on the strength of it.
Leading/trailing whitespace collapses then trims; first letter capitalizes.

Spanish opens a question with an inverted mark. The capitalizer upper-cases the first CHARACTER after a sentence boundary; '¿' has no uppercase form, so without an opener rule the real first letter stays lowercase. SENTENCE_OPENERS = '¿¡' only — quotes/brackets are NOT openers (they also close, and capitalizing after them would mangle list markers).
Opener sits between the sentence-ending punctuation and the first letter. Covers both inverted marks.

An opener binds to the word it opens: '¿ qué' -> '¿qué'. This spacing pass MUST run before capitalization, so the capitalizer sees the real first letter and not a space. The second input ('¿cómo', no space) proves the rule is not merely a whitespace artefact.
The plugin's primary output is HTML paragraphs, so an opener after a block-level tag is the commonest real case of all.
Multi-line templates hit the newline capitalization rule rather than the sentence-punctuation one.

Guards the deliberate NARROWNESS of SENTENCE_OPENERS. A quote or bracket is not an opener: capitalizing after one would break list markers like '(a) primero'. If this case ever starts capitalizing, the contract was widened by accident.

Cross-engine guard for the NARROWNESS of SENTENCE_OPENERS: a quote is not an opener. Both straight (") and guillemet («) forms stay lowercase after a sentence boundary, while the start-of-text capitalisation still fires — so the rule is proven to be narrow rather than simply dead. A TS unit test alone would not bind the PHP engine; this is the parity gate. Companion to postprocess/opener-set-excludes-quotes-and-brackets, which guards the bracket case.

RAE's form for a sentence that is both a question and an exclamation opens with TWO marks. A lead that allows exactly one opener leaves the most Spanish construction there is uncapitalized — and the closing '?!' is a run, so it must survive the spacing pass intact too. Both halves of the defect are visible in this one case.
The other order RAE sanctions. Locks that the lead is a RUN of openers rather than a hardcoded '¡¿' pair.

The opened word is routinely wrapped in markup, which puts a tag AFTER the opener. The lead has to allow tags on BOTH sides of it: 'boundary → tags → opener → letter' was handled, 'boundary → opener → tags → letter' was not.
The commonest real shape of all: an HTML paragraph whose Spanish question opens with a link. Exercises the block-tag capitalizer through an opener followed by an anchor.

A run of sentence punctuation is ONE sentence end, not several. The 'space after .!?' rule fired between the marks and shredded the copy in EVERY language: 'Wait... what' became 'Wait. . . what'. The Unicode '…' was never in the [.!?] class and so was never affected — which is exactly why the corpus's ellipsis fixture missed this.
A run that ends the text gets no trailing space. Guards the backtracking trap: a greedy '+' alone still backs INTO the run to satisfy the lookaheads, yielding 'Wow!! !'.
'?!' is one sentence end: it must not be split, and the capitalizer must still fire on the word after it.
The space belongs AFTER the whole run, never inside it — so a word glued to the run is separated from it, once.

A URI body runs to the first delimiter, so a mailto: carrying a URL overlaps the URL rule. Shielding them in two passes let the second run into the placeholder the first had minted; the swallowed key never restored and the engine emitted a raw U+0000 on input that carried none (spintax-js#53). The whole token must shield as one.
The comma is inside the URI body class, so 'tel:…,https://…' is a single token and the 'space after ,' rule must not reach into it. Same defect as the mailto: case, reached through the other scheme.

Restore must substitute the tokens the shield placed, not every occurrence of their text. Here the shield leaves <NUL>URL_0<NUL> <NUL>ABBR_2<NUL>URL_0<NUL>URI_1<NUL>: ABBR_2's closing delimiter, the author's literal 'URL_0' and URI_1's opening delimiter spell a third occurrence of URL_0's key, because delimiters are not owned by the token that placed them. A restore that replaces each key across the whole text substitutes the forgery and destroys two real tokens, returning raw U+0000 from input that carries none. No U+0000 is needed in the input to reach this — only prose that names a placeholder, which any document about this engine does (spintax-js#54).

NEGATIVE case, guarding the mirror direction: a URL whose path carries a mailto:. Fixing the case above by shielding mailto: BEFORE urls passes that one and breaks this one — the URL is split and its leading half loses the trailing dot to the punctuation pass ('https://x.io/a. mailto:…'). Both directions hold only if the two schemes shield in one pass.

A Cyrillic multi-dot abbreviation is shielded exactly like 'e.g.': step 5a's leading \b is PHP's under /u, and /u is PCRE2_UCP, so a letter of any script is a word character. Every tree-walk engine had an ASCII \b here and rendered 'и т. Д. И т. П. Всё'.
template: яблоки, груши и т.д. и т.п. всё

expect.output: Яблоки, груши и т.д. и т.п. всё

note: The spaced form of step 5a ((?:\p{L}{1,2}\.\s*){2,}): 'т. е.' is one abbreviation, so neither 'е' nor the next word is capitalized.

A domain in its Unicode form is shielded — §5 names IDN beside ASCII and punycode (the punycode twin of this one is postprocess/punycode-domain-shielded). The leading \b before 'пример' exists only because PHP's \b is UCP.
The email shield ends in \b as well. With an ASCII \b the TLD 'рф' has no boundary after it, the address goes unshielded, and the punctuation pass splits it: 'info@сайт. Рф'.
An ASCII label under a Cyrillic TLD: the boundary AFTER the domain is the UCP one too.
Step 7 removes \s+ before punctuation, and PHP's \s is UCP: a no-break space before the comma goes like a space would.
(?!\s|$|<) sees the no-break space, so no second space is inserted after the comma.
A no-break space after a full stop is whitespace to the spacing pass (nothing inserted) and to the capitalization lead (the next word is capitalized).
Russian typesetting binds 'тыс.' and 'руб.' with a no-break space. The whitelist lookahead (?=\s|$|<) has to see it, or 'тыс.' is not shielded and the spacing pass adds a second space.
The URI body class excludes \s, which is UCP in PHP: a no-break space ends the URL, and what follows is spaced and capitalized as ordinary text.
(?!\d) is UCP in PHP — any decimal digit, \p{Nd}; here ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE — so no space is inserted after the comma, as with an ASCII digit.
U+0085 (NEL) is \s under PCRE2_UCP but NOT in JavaScript's \s — an engine porting the class from JS gets this one wrong. Nothing is inserted after the stop, and the next word is capitalized.

NEGATIVE, the mirror of postprocess/nel-is-whitespace: U+FEFF is \s in JavaScript but NOT under PCRE2_UCP. So a space is inserted after the stop and the next word stays lowercase, the character between them not counting as a gap.

Pinned as both PHP engines render it, not as a verdict on it: 'конец.Начало' matches the bare-domain shield — a label and a TLD of 2+ letters, UCP boundaries on both sides — so the missing space is not inserted and nothing is capitalized, exactly as 'compact.Game' in ASCII. Whether the shield should take a capitalized TLD at all is spintax-js#79; deciding that moves this fixture.

The boundary seen from the other side: UCP \w includes '_' AND every letter, so there is no boundary between '_' and 'т' and the multi-dot shield does not fire. An engine with an ASCII \b saw one there and shielded '_т.д.'.
